note: Part C: synthetic paragraphs written for Researchly's Laya critic (2026-10-16): social sciences, humanities, health policy and other genres. Original text, invented data, no real people's names. Licence: ours.

paragraphs.text: Over the last few years there has been a growing amount of interest in the topic of platform-based gig work and the ways in which it affects the everyday lives of the people who carry it out. Food delivery riders in particular have become a highly visible part of the urban landscape in many cities. This has led to a number of debates about whether this kind of work should be considered as employment or as self-employment. However, there is a lack of studies that look at how riders themselves make sense of their working time. This study aims to address this.

Rural secondary schools in the hill districts face a persistent shortage of qualified mathematics teachers, and the shortage is worst in the schools that serve the poorest households. Government schemes have tried to close the gap by posting contract teachers on short renewable terms, but contract posts are filled slowly and vacated quickly. We know a good deal about how many posts are vacant; we know far less about what happens inside a classroom during the months a post stands empty. This thesis examines those months. It asks how head teachers, remaining staff and students reorganise mathematics teaching when no specialist is present, and what that reorganisation costs students who sit the board examination at the end of the year.

Loneliness among older adults is widely recognised as a public health concern, with consequences for both mental and physical health. Most of the existing research on this topic have been conducted in high-income countries, and it is often assumed that the findings transfer unchanged to settings where older people typically live with extended family. This assumption is rarely tested. Living with others does not guarantee being heard by them, and an older person can be surrounded by relatives yet feel that nobody asks for their opinion. The present study investigates loneliness among older adults living in multigenerational households in two mid-sized towns.

The implementation of the introduction of minimum unit pricing for alcohol represents a significant intervention in the regulation of alcohol markets. The evaluation of the effectiveness of this policy has been the subject of considerable discussion. It is clearly the case that higher prices reduce consumption overall. However, the distribution of the effects of the policy across different income groups is less well understood, and this is important because it is the heaviest drinkers on lowest incomes who experience the greatest burden of alcohol-related harm.

Historians of the nineteenth-century textile industry have long treated the mill town as the natural unit of analysis, reconstructing wages, strikes and housing one town at a time. Such studies have given us rich portraits of particular places, but they leave open a question that matters for any account of how workers organised: how far did information, rumour and money travel between towns during a dispute? Letters, strike-fund ledgers and railway parcel records survive in scattered county archives, and taken together they allow the movement of support between towns to be traced week by week. This chapter uses them to follow one regional dispute from its first walk-out to its collapse eleven months later.

Informed consent is a cornerstone of research ethics. But in community-based research, the idea of consent as an individual signature on a form often sit uneasily with how decisions are actually made. In many villages, a researcher who approaches a household without first speaking to elders may be seen as disrespectful, and the household may agree to take part only because they feel they cannot refuse an outsider. This raises a important question about what consent means in such settings. Few empirical studies has examined how participants themselves understand the consent process.

Unemployment insurance is designed to smooth consumption when workers lose their jobs, but generous benefits may also lengthen the time people spend searching for new work. Economists have estimated this trade-off many times using administrative data from Europe and North America. Far fewer estimates exists for middle-income countries, where informal work offers an alternative to formal job search and where benefit schemes are newer. In this paper we use a reform that extended benefit duration for workers above a certain age threshold to estimate how benefit duration affects time to re-employment and the quality of the next job.

It is widely believed that mindfulness interventions improve the wellbeing of university students. Many universities now offer mindfulness courses as part of there student support services. However the evidence base is mixed. Some trials report large effects, others report none, and a number of trials are small and at high risk of bias. Moreover, very few trials have followed students for longer than a single term. It is therefore unclear whether any benefits persist. This gap in the litterature is what motivated the present study, which follows students for a full academic year.

Out-of-pocket spending on medicines remains the largest single component of household health expenditure in many low- and middle-income countries. When a family member falls ill, households may borrow money, sell assets or simply go without treatment. This can push households into poverty, and it can also cause families to delay care until a condition becomes more serious and more expensive to treat. Free medicine schemes in public facilities are intended to break this cycle, but stock-outs mean that patients are often sent to private pharmacies anyway. Our study asks how often this happens and what it costs.

Teachers' beliefs about intelligence shape what they expect from their students and, through those expectations, how they teach. A teacher who believes that ability is fixed may give fewer challenging tasks to students labelled as weak; a teacher who believes that ability grows with effort may persist longer with the same students. These ideas have been studied extensively in psychology, but mostly through questionnaires completed by teachers in a single moment. Little is known about whether teachers express the same beliefs when they talk about real students in their own classrooms, where the beliefs must coexist with pressure to cover the syllabus.

The present study is an attempt to understand the role of self help groups (SHGs) in the empowerment of rural women in the state. SHGs have been promoted by government as well as NGOs since the 1990s. Till date, many studies have discussed about the economic benefits of SHG membership, such as access to credit. But the social dimensions of empowerment like decision making in household, mobility and participation in village meetings has received comparatively less attention. The present study will try to fill up this gap by collecting data from 240 SHG members in two blocks of the district.

Over the past two decades, governments have increasingly turned to behavioural insights to design public policy. Defaults, reminders and simplified forms are now routinely tested in randomised trials run by dedicated units inside ministries. These tools are attractive because they are cheap, but critics argue that they shift attention away from structural causes of disadvantage. This tension is visible in debates about tax compliance, pension saving and organ donation. In this article we focus on a less studied area, namely appointment reminders in public dental services, where high DNA rates waste clinical time and lengthen waiting lists for everyone else.

Moral distress, the experience of knowing the right thing to do but being unable to do it, has been described among nurses for more than three decades. It is associated with burnout, intention to leave, and lower quality of care. During periods of severe staffing pressure, nurses may be forced to ration their attention between patients in ways that conflict with their professional values. While the concept is well established in nursing ethics, it has been applied far less often to community health workers, whose role is defined by close and long-term relationships with households rather than with hospital wards.

The question of why some countries adopted universal health coverage earlier than others has attracted attention from political scientists and from health policy scholars, although the two literatures rarely speak to each other. Political scientists tend to emphasise electoral competition and the strength of left parties; health policy scholars emphasise the role of technocrats and international organisations. Neither account, on its own, explains the timing of reform in the three cases examined in this thesis, each of which passed legislation in a year without an election and against the advice of the main international lender. I argue that the missing piece is the bargaining between finance ministries and the medical profession over who would pay providers and on what terms.

Its well known that students from lower socio-economic backgrounds are less likely to apply to selective universities, even when they have the grades to be admitted. This phenomenon, sometimes called undermatching, has been documented in several countries. Information interventions which tell high-achieving students about financial aid have been shown to increase applications in some settings. However it is not clear whether students who are nudged in this way go on to complete their degrees, or whether they drop out at higher rates once they arrive. This is an important question for policy, since the purpose of widening participation is completion and not just enrolment.

Thematic analysis has become one of the most commonly used approaches in qualitative health research. Its flexibility is often cited as a strength: it is not tied to a particular theoretical framework and can be applied to interviews, focus groups and written responses alike. That flexibility, however, has also led to considerable variation in how the method is reported. Papers describe 'themes emerging' from data without explaining who identified them or how, and the distinction between a theme and a topic summary is frequently blurred. This paper reviews reporting practices in a sample of published qualitative studies of patient experience.

Climate anxiety has emerged as a term to describe distress about climate change, particularly among young people. Surveys report that a large proportion of adolescents feels worried, sad or angry about the future of the planet. Yet it remains contested whether such feelings should be understood as a clinical problem, as a rational response to a real threat, or as a motivating force for collective action. Each framing carries different implications for schools and for mental health services. This study explores how secondary school teachers in three regions respond when students raise climate distress in the classroom.

The utilisation of digital payment systems by small retailers has increased substantially following the demonetisation of high-value currency notes. The adoption of such systems has implications for the formalisation of the economy, for the collection of tax and for the financial inclusion of small business owners. This undoubtedly proves that digital payments are transforming the informal sector. However, there is limited research on the experiences of retailers who discontinued the use of digital payments after an initial period of adoption, and on the reasons for their discontinuation.

Why do some refugees settle in the first city they reach while others move on within a year? Resettlement agencies plan housing, language classes and job placement on the assumption that families will stay where they are placed, and secondary migration is often treated as a sign that integration has failed. Yet families may move for good reasons: to join relatives, to find work that matches their skills, or to reach a school that teaches in a language their children already know. This study follows 86 households over two years after placement to describe who moves, when, and what they said about their reasons.

Previous research has shown that adolescent sleep is affected by school start times. Studies conducted in the United States suggests that delaying the start of the school day by as little as thirty minutes can increase total sleep time. Studies conducted in the United States also suggest effects on attendance and mood. However these studies are mostly from the United States and it is not known whether the results apply in other countries where school days are organized differently. We therefore conducted a study in a different country. The aim of this study is to examine whether a later start time was associated with longer sleep.

Archives are never neutral repositories of the past. What survives, and in what order, reflects decisions taken by clerks, collectors and later cataloguers, many of whom had their own views about which records mattered. For historians of colonial public health, this means that the voices of patients, midwives and village vaccinators are often available only through the reports of the officials who supervised them. The present chapter reads a set of district sanitary reports against the grain, attending less to the officers' conclusions than to the incidental remarks, complaints and marginal corrections through which other people's actions become visible.

The burden of mental health conditions among adolescents has grown substantially, and in many countries services for young people are unable to meet demand. School-based counselling is one response that has been widely adopted. In order to be able to assess whether or not school counselling services are achieving their intended aims, it is necessary for there to be a clear understanding of what it is that counsellors actually do in their sessions with students. At the present moment in time, such understanding is limited. This study therefore aims to describe the content of school counselling sessions.

Housing first programmes offer permanent housing to people experiencing chronic homelessness without requiring them to first achieve sobriety or engage with treatment. Evaluations in several countries have reported high rates of housing retention. Less is known about what happens to participants' social networks once they are housed, particularly whether they keep contact with friends who remain on the street. These networks may provide support, but they can also expose tenants to pressure that puts their tenancy at risk. In this paper we use repeated network interviews with 41 tenants to examine how their personal networks changed during the first eighteen months of housing.

We set out in this thesis to examine how primary care doctors make decisions about antibiotic prescribing for respiratory infections in private clinics. It is known that antibiotic prescribing is higher in private than public facilities. I suggest that patient expectations are only part of the explanation. Clinic owners may set consultation targets, and doctors may worry that a patient sent home without a prescription will not come back. We conducted interviews with 32 doctors, and I also observed consultations in six clinics. Our findings suggest that commercial pressures and patient expectations interact in complex ways.

Vaccine hesitancy is a complex and context-specific phenomenon which varies across time, place and vaccines. It is extremely important and absolutely crucial for public health practitioners to understand the reasons behind hesitancy, because hesitancy can lead to outbreaks of preventable disease. Some studies show that trust in health workers is the single most important determinant of vaccine acceptance and this definitively demonstrates that trust-building should be the priority of all immunisation programmes. However, few studies have looked at trust among parents in urban informal settlements.

The minimum wage has been studied by economists for a long time. There are many studies. Some find that raising it reduces employment. Others find no effect. The debate continues. This paper looks at the effect of a regional minimum wage increase on hours worked by part-time workers in retail. This is relevant because part-time workers may see their hours cut even if they keep their jobs. We use payroll data from a large employer. Results show that hours fell slightly.

Parents' involvement in their children's schooling is consistently associated with better outcomes, but the term covers activities that have little in common: helping with homework, attending meetings, talking about school at dinner, and holding high expectations. Studies that combine these activities into a single index cannot tell schools which of them to encourage. Moreover, the forms of involvement that schools find easiest to see, such as attendance at parent evenings, are the ones least available to parents who work shifts. The present study separates these forms and asks which are associated with reading progress in the first two years of primary school, in a sample where a third of parents work irregular hours.

Within the sociology of professions, the concept of jurisdiction has been used to explain how occupations claim and defend areas of work. Nurses, pharmacists and physician assistants have all expanded their scope of practice in recent decades, often over the objections of medical associations. These contests are usually studied at the level of national legislation. Yet the boundaries of a profession are also negotiated daily on hospital wards, in conversations about who may adjust a dose or order a test. The present article examines these everyday negotiations in two hospitals, one in which nurse prescribing had been formally introduced and one in which it had not.

Despite decades of policy attention, the gender gap in STEM degree completion persists in many countries. Explanations have focused variously on early socialisation, stereotype threat, the culture of particular disciplines, and the absence of role models. Each of these explanations has some empirical support. Few studies, however, have followed women through the specific transition from the first to the second year of an engineering degree, which institutional data suggest is where most departures occur. Using enrolment records for six cohorts and interviews with 28 students who left, this paper examines what happens at that point.

Conditional cash transfers (CCTs) have been adopted in more than sixty countries as a way to raise school attendance among poor children. The evidence that CCTs increase enrolment is strong. Whether the extra schooling translates into learning is much less clear, and some evaluations finds no gain in test scores at all. One explanation is that the additional pupils enter classrooms that are already overcrowded. Another is that the cash transfer changes who attends without changing what happens in class. The LSMS data used in this paper allow us to look at the cash payments together with classroom size, and to ask whether the effect of the conditional transfers on learning depends on how crowded the receiving school was.

I conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 delivery riders between March and August. Riders were recruited at three restaurant clusters where they waited between orders, and through a messaging group that one early participant invited me to join. Interviews lasted between 35 and 90 minutes and were held wherever riders felt comfortable, usually a tea stall or a parked bike. I audio-recorded the interviews with permission and transcribed them myself, translating from Hindi where needed. I kept a reflexive diary throughout, noting how my own position as a university researcher who had never done delivery work shaped what riders chose to tell me.

Data were analysed using thematic analysis following the six phases described by Braun and Clarke. Firstly, the transcripts were read and re-read in order to achieve familiarisation with the data. Then initial codes were generated in NVivo. Codes was then collated into potential themes, and the themes were reviewed against the coded extracts and against the full data set. Themes was then defined and named. The analysis is conducted by the first author, and a second researcher coded 20% of transcripts independently. Disagreements were discussed until consensus is reached.

The survey was administered to all Year 9 students in the twelve participating schools during a regular lesson. Students completed the questionnaire on paper, and teachers were asked to remain at the front of the room so that they could not see responses. The questionnaire took around 25 minutes to complete. It included the 10-item version of the perceived stress scale, a short measure of school belonging, and questions on sleep, screen use and part-time work. Of 1,412 students on the rolls, 1,236 completed the questionnaire (87.5%). Students who were absent on the day were not followed up.

The study was carried out in two blocks of the district which were selected purposively. A multi-stage sampling was adopted for the selection of respondents. In the first stage, 8 villages were selected randomly from each block. In the second stage, 15 SHG members were selected from each village by using simple random sampling, thus making a total sample of 240 respondents. The respondents were explained about the purpose of the study and their consent was taken. The data was collected with the help of a pre-tested interview schedule in the local language. The data was analysed by using percentages, chi square test and Garrett ranking technique.

We estimate the effect of benefit duration on unemployment duration using a regression discontinuity design. Workers who lost their jobs at age 40 or above became eligible for 12 months of benefits, while younger workers were eligible for 6 months. We restrict the sample to workers aged between 35 and 45 at the time of job loss and estimate local linear regressions on each side of the threshold, using the bandwidth selector proposed by Calonico and co-authors. Standard errors are clustered at the level of age in months. We test for manipulation of the running variable using a density test and find no evidence of bunching at the threshold.

Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the university's research ethics committee. All participants gave written informed consent prior to participation. Participants were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any time without giving a reason. In order to ensure the protection of the confidentiality of participants, all names were replaced by pseudonyms and identifying details were removed from the transcripts. It should be noted that the data were stored on an encrypted drive which was password-protected. It is also important to note that only the members of the research team had access to the data.

The archive of the district sanitary commissioner contains 214 annual and quarterly reports for the period 1871 to 1912. I read every report in full, rather than sampling, because the incidental remarks that interested me could appear anywhere: in a table footnote, in a complaint about a vaccinator's pay, or in a paragraph about the weather. For each report I recorded every mention of a named or unnamed subordinate worker, the action attributed to them, and the officer's evaluation of that action. I then read these entries chronologically, looking for changes in vocabulary and for moments where the officers' complaints implied that subordinates had acted independently.

A convergent mixed methods design was used. The quantitative strand consisted of a cross-sectional survey of 410 caregivers; the qualitative strand consisted of 18 in-depth interviews with caregivers purposively sampled from the survey participants to include both those with high and low scores on the trust scale. The two strands were collected in parallel and analyzed separately, and then they was integrated using a joint display in which each survey finding is placed alongside the interview themes which related to it. Where the two strands disagreed, we returned to the transcripts to look for an explanation.

Participants were recruited through posters in the student union, and through emails send by course administrators. Eligible students were aged 18 or over, enrolled full-time, and had not practised meditation regularly in the previous six months. After a baseline assessment, participants were randomised to an eight-week mindfulness course or to a waitlist control using a computer-generated sequence with blocks of varying size. The allocation was concealed from the researchers who conducted the assessments. Outcomes were measured at baseline, at the end of the course, and at six and twelve months. The primary outcome is psychological distress measured by the CORE-10.

Focus groups were conducted with parents in each of the four schools. Each group had between five and nine participants and was facilitated by two researchers, one of whom led the discussion while the other took notes on interaction and who spoke. A topic guide was used, but facilitators were encouraged to follow up on issues that parents raised themselves. Groups were held in the evening and childcare was provided. We offered a shopping voucher to thank participants for their time, which some parents declined.

Our primary outcome is the number of days between job loss and the start of a new formal-sector job, measured from the social security register. Workers who do not return to formal employment within 36 months is treated as censored. The secondary outcomes are the log of the monthly wage in the new job, and whether the new job was with an employer in the same two-digit industry. Since the register does not record informal work, a worker who leaves the register may have found informal employment, left the labour force or emigrated; we discuss the implications of this for interpretation in Section 6.

The interviews were conducted in English or in Twi, depending on the preference of the participant, and they lasted on average 50 minutes. The interviewer was a trained research assistant who was fluent in both languages. Interviews in Twi were transcribed and translated into English by the same research assistant, and a random sample of 5 transcripts was back-translated by a second translator to check the accuracy of the translation. Minor differences in wording was found but no differences in meaning. Because of the sensitive nature of some of the topics discussed, the research assistant was trained in how to respond if a participant became distressed.

To examine the association between parental involvement and reading progress, multilevel linear regression models were fitted with children nested within classrooms. Reading progress was defined as the difference between the standardised reading score at the end of Year 2 and at entry. Four forms of involvement were entered as separate predictors. Models were adjusted for child age, sex, eligibility for free school meals, and home language. The intraclass correlation for classrooms was 0.11. Missing data on covariates (8% of children) was handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputed datasets.

The current study utilised a qualitative descriptive design. A total of 15 participants were interviewed. The sample size was determined by data saturation, which was reached after 12 interviews, and three further interviews were conducted to confirm that no new themes emerged. The interviews were semi-structured in nature and were conducted face to face in a private room within the health facility. The duration of the interviews ranged from 30 to 55 minutes. The interviews was audio recorded and transcribed verbatim. Field notes was also taken.

We used a difference-in-differences design that compares changes in alcohol purchases between households in the region that introduced the minimum price and households in neighbouring regions that did not. Purchase data comes from a consumer panel in which households scan every item they bring home. We define the pre-period as the 24 months before implementation and the post-period as the 24 months after it. Our main specification includes household and month fixed effects. To examine heterogeneity, we interact the treatment indicator with household income tercile and with baseline purchasing, defined as alcohol units bought per adult in the pre-period.

Following an initial open coding of the first ten transcripts, I developed a coding frame which I then applied to all transcripts, adding new codes where the frame did not fit. I want to be clear that the themes reported below did not simply emerge from the data; they reflect my questions, my reading of the literature on moral distress, and decisions I made about which differences between participants mattered. To keep those decisions visible, I wrote an analytic memo after coding each transcript and discussed the developing themes with two colleagues who had worked as community health workers before entering research.

Network data was collected using a name generator. Participants were asked to name up to 15 people with whom they had discussed important matters, spent time socially, or borrowed or lent money in the previous three months. For each person named participants were asked about their relationship, how often they were in contact, and wether the person was currently housed. The same name generator was used at baseline, six months, twelve months and eighteen months. Alters named at more than one wave were matched by the interviewer by using first name, relationship and approximate age, which inevitably introduces some errors in matching which we discuss later.

The sample comprised of 186 undergraduate students enrolled in a first-year psychology course, who took part in exchange for course credit. Participants completed an online questionnaire which measured their mindset beliefs, academic self-efficacy and test anxiety, followed by a timed problem-solving task. Half of the participants were randomly allocated to read a short article on brain plasticity before the task, while the other half read an article on the history of the university. Data was cleaned and analysed in R. Six participants who failed both attention checks were excluded, leaving a final sample of 180.

Document analysis was carried out on 47 policy documents published by the health ministry between 2005 and 2020, including strategic plans, annual reports and circulars. Documents were identified through the ministry website and through requests to the policy unit. Each document was coded for the stated objectives of the health insurance scheme, the population groups mentioned, and the indicators proposed for monitoring progress. We were interested both in what the documents said and in what they left out; for example, whether informal-sector workers were named explicitly or were included only within broader categories.

Observations was carried out in six private clinics over a period of four months. With the consent of the doctor and the patient, I sat in the consultation room and recorded, on a structured form, the presenting complaint, the duration of the consultation, whether the patient asked for a specific medicine, and what was prescribed. I did not record names. I also wrote free-text notes on the conversation. In total, 412 consultations were observed. Doctors knew that I was interested in prescribing, which may have changed their behaviour; this is discussed in the limitations.

The survey instrument was developed in several stages. Firstly, items were drawn from existing validated scales where possible. Secondly, new items were written to capture aspects of trust in community health volunteers, which the existing scales did not cover. Thirdly, the draft instrument was reviewed by a panel of six experts. Fourthly, it was piloted with 30 caregivers in a neighbouring district, and items with low variance or that respondents found confusing was removed or reworded. The final instrument contained 42 items. Cronbach's alpha for the trust subscale was 0.84.

Interviews explored participants' experiences of seeking care for their child's most recent illness. Participants were first asked to describe what happened, in their own words, from the moment they noticed the child was unwell. Follow-up questions asked about who they consulted, where they obtained medicines and how they paid. We avoided asking directly about trust, because pilot interviews showed that a direct question produced polite, general answers. Instead, trust was explored through accounts of specific encounters.

Archival research was supplemented by oral history interviews with eleven former mill workers and their descendants, conducted in their homes. These interviews are used with caution. Memories of events that happened sixty or more years ago, often passed down second-hand, are shaped by later events and by the stories communities tell about themselves. I treat the interviews not as evidence of what happened in the dispute, but as evidence of how the dispute is remembered, and I use them alongside the documentary record rather than in place of it.

The intervention consisted of text message reminders sent to patients three days and one day before their dental appointment. Patients were randomised individually to one of three arms: no reminder (control), a standard reminder stating the time and place, and a reminder which additionally stated the cost to the service of a missed appointment. Randomisation was stratified by clinic. The primary outcome was attendance at the scheduled appointment, as recorded on the clinic's booking system. The trial was registered prospectively. The sample size of 3,600 patients were calculated to detect a reduction in missed appointments from 15% to 11% with 90% power.

Each interview was transcribed verbatim, including pauses, laughter and false starts, because the way participants talked about consent was as revealing as what they said. Transcripts were imported into ATLAS.ti. The coding was done in two cycles. In the first cycle, descriptive codes were attached to segments of text. In the second cycle, these codes were grouped into broader patterns. The analysis was iterative, in that the coding of later interviews shaped how earlier interviews were reread. It were not possible to return transcripts to participants for checking, as many lacked a stable address.

Data were drawn from the national household budget survey for the years 2011, 2016 and 2021. Catastrophic health expenditure was defined as out-of-pocket health spending exceeding 10% of total household consumption. As a sensitivity analysis, we also used a threshold of 25% and a capacity-to-pay definition which substracts food spending from the denominator. Households were classified as having been impoverished by health spending if their consumption was above the national poverty line before out-of-pocket payments and below it after. All estimates were weighted to account for the survey design.

For this study, the researcher adopted a phenomenological approach because the aim was to understand the lived experiences of the participants. Phenomenology is concerned with the essence of an experience as it is lived. In this study, we used purposive sampling to recruit 12 nurses who had worked in intensive care units during the pandemic. The researcher conducted the interviews online. We believe that this gave participants the comfort of being in their own homes. The researcher then analysed the data using interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA).

Teacher talk about students was collected in two ways. First, we audio-recorded the regular weekly planning meetings in each school's mathematics department over one term, yielding 41 hours of recordings. Second, we conducted stimulus-based interviews in which teachers were shown anonymised work from three of their own students and asked to describe each student's progress and prospects. We transcribed all recordings and coded each statement about a student's ability using a scheme adapted from earlier questionnaire studies, distinguishing statements that located ability in the student as a fixed property from statements that linked it to effort, teaching or circumstances.

Participants were 62 adults aged 65 and over who lived in households with at least two other generations. They were recruited via primary health centres, temples and a pensioner's association. The UCLA loneliness scale was administered orally by trained interviewers, since many participants could not read. In addition, a subsample of 20 participants took part in an in-depth interview about their daily routines and relationships within the household. Interviews were conducted in Marathi, translated and transcribed by bilingual research assistant. The quantitative data were analyzed in SPSS and the qualitative data was analysed thematically.

Enrolment records for six cohorts of engineering students (n = 3,941) was obtained from the university's planning office under a data sharing agreement. Records included gender, entry qualifications, programme, and enrolment status at the start of each semester. Departure was defined as not being enrolled at the start of the third semester and not having transferred to another programme. To recruit interviewees, the university emailed all women who met this definition in the three most recent cohorts on our behalf; 28 agreed to take part. We did not have access to contact details for students who did not respond.

Riders described their working day not in hours but in orders. Several riders said that they set themselves a target number of deliveries and would not go home until they reached it, regardless of how long this took. As one rider put it, "the app doesn't know I have a family, it only knows if I'm online." Waiting time between orders was experienced as the most frustrating part of the day, because it was unpaid but could not be used for anything else. This clearly shows that platform work erodes the boundary between work and life for all riders.

Of the 240 respondents, majority (68.3%) were in the age group of 31–45 years. Most of the respondents were married (87.5%) and belonged to OBC category (52.1%). Regarding the educational status, 34.6% were illiterate, 41.2% had studied upto primary level and only 24.2% had studied above primary. The table 2 reveals that after joining SHG, there is a significant increase in the participation of women in decision making regarding children's education (χ² = 18.4, p < 0.01). The same is also observed in decisions regarding purchase of household assets.

Students in the mindfulness arm reported lower psychological distress than those in the waitlist arm at the end of the course (mean difference −2.1 points on the CORE-10, 95% CI −3.0 to −1.2). At six months the difference was smaller (−1.2, 95% CI −2.2 to −0.2), and at twelve months it was close to zero (−0.4, 95% CI −1.5 to 0.7). Attendance at the course was modest: 58% of participants attended at least four of the eight sessions. In a per-protocol analysis restricted to these participants the end-of-course difference was larger (−3.0), but this analysis does not preserve randomisation and should be interpreted cautiously.

There were three main themes which were identified in the analysis of the data. These were "knowing the household", "being caught in between" and "carrying it home". The first theme, knowing the household, related to the long-term relationships which CHWs had with the families they visited. Participants describes how they knew which families would follow advice and which would not. The second theme related to the experience of being caught between the expectations of the households and the expectations of supervisors. This was described as very stressful by most participants.

The estimated discontinuity in unemployment duration at the age-40 threshold is 41 days (standard error 12), meaning that workers eligible for 12 months of benefits took about six weeks longer to return to formal employment than workers just below the threshold. The effect is concentrated among workers with below-median earnings in their previous job. We find no discontinuity in the wage of the next job (Table 3), and a small but imprecisely estimated increase in the probability of returning to the same industry. Estimates are stable across bandwidths between half and twice the optimal bandwidth (Figure A2).

Table 4 presents the result of the multilevel models. Of the four forms of involvement, only talking about school at home were associated with reading progress after adjustment (β = 0.12 SD, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.19). Attendance at parent meetings were not associated with progress (β = 0.02, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.09), nor were help with homework (β = −0.03, 95% CI −0.10 to 0.04). Interestingly, help with homework had a negative point estimate. This may be because parents help more when their child is struggling.

In the first two months of the dispute, the strike-fund ledger records remittances from nine towns, most of them within a day's rail journey. From the third month the pattern changes. Remittances from the nearest towns decline, apparently because their own mills had begun short-time working, while small sums begin to arrive from much further away, including two ports and a mining district with no textile industry at all. The correspondence that accompanies these sums suggests that they were collected at chapel meetings and public houses rather than by unions, and several letters ask the strike committee to send a speaker in return.

The overall prevalence of catastrophic health expenditure at the 10% threshold decreased from 14.2% in 2011 to 11.8% in 2016 and was 12.6% in 2021 (Table 2). The decrease between 2011 and 2016 were concentrated in urban households. Among rural households in the poorest quintile, prevalence actually increased over the whole period, from 16.1% to 19.4%. Medicines accounted for the largest share of out-of-pocket spending in all three years, between 61% and 67%. The proportion of households impoverished by health spending followed a similar pattern.

Most participants described the consent process as something that had happened to the household rather than to them as individuals. Several women said that their husband or mother-in-law had agreed on their behalf before they had been approached, and that they then signed because "it was already decided". Others described signing as a sign of politeness to a visitor: "You don't refuse someone who has come all this way." Only a few participants mentioned the information sheet. This finding demonstrates that individual consent is meaningless in these communities and should be replaced by community consent.

Teachers made 1,184 statements about students' ability across the planning meetings and interviews. In the interviews, where teachers were discussing named students and their work, 61% of statements linked ability to effort, teaching or circumstances. In the planning meetings, where teachers were discussing sets and timetabling, the figure was 34%. The same teachers therefore expressed markedly different beliefs in the two contexts. Fixed-ability statements in planning meetings clustered around decisions about which set a student should move to, and were often phrased in terms of what a student "can cope with".

The reminder messages reduced missed appointments. In the control arm, 15.3% of appointments was missed, compared with 12.1% in the standard reminder arm and 10.4% in the cost reminder arm. The difference between the cost reminder and the standard reminder (1.7 percentage points, 95% CI 0.2 to 3.2) was smaller then the difference between either reminder and the control. Effects were similar across clinics. There was no evidence that the cost message increased cancellations rather than attendance: cancellation rates was 6.2%, 6.8% and 6.5% respectively.

In terms of the results of the analysis of the survey data, it was found that there was a statistically significant association between the level of trust in community health volunteers and the likelihood of the completion of the full vaccination schedule (adjusted odds ratio 1.8, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.7). It was also found that there was an association between the level of education of the caregiver and trust, with caregivers with secondary education being more likely to report high levels of trust. However, it was found that there was no association between distance to the health facility and trust.

Among the 41 tenants, the median size of personal networks fell from 9 at baseline to 6 at eighteen months. The decline was almost entirely in ties to people who were still homeless: at baseline these made up 52% of named alters; at eighteen months, 23%. New ties formed during the period were mostly with service staff and with neighbours. Ten tenants kept atleast one close tie with a person still on the street throughout the study, and several of them described this as a source of both support and worry. Two tenants lost their tenancies during the study; both had invited friends to stay.

Retailers who had discontinued digital payments gave a range of reasons. The most common reason, mentioned by 37 of the 52 retailers interviewed, was the delay in settlement, as money received digitally took between one and three days to reach their bank account while their suppliers demanded cash. Transaction charges was mentioned by 21 retailers. Fear of tax scrutiny was mentioned by 14, although retailers often attributed this fear to others ("people say the tax office will see everything") rather than to themselves. This shows that tax fear is the hidden reason behind discontinuation.

Figure 2 shows the proportion of women leaving after the first year by cohort. Departure rates were higher for women than for men in every cohort, the gap ranged from 3 to 9 percentage points. Women who left had, on average, higher entry qualifications than men who left, which argues against the explanation that they were less prepared academically. In interviews, the most frequently discussed experience was the first-year group design project. Women described being assigned to note-taking and presentation tasks while men in the group did the technical work, as one put it "I was the secretary of my own project."

Loneliness scores were higher among older adults who had been widowed (mean 47.2, SD 8.1) than among those who were married (mean 41.5, SD 7.6). Scores were also higher among participants who did not have their own room, and among women compared with men. Living with a larger number of family members was not associated with lower loneliness. In the interviews, participants who reported high loneliness often described being excluded from family decisions, such as arrangements for a grandchild's wedding. One participant said that she was "consulted about the menu and nothing else".

Doctors described the decision to prescribe an antibiotic as rarely about the clinical picture alone. In 29 of the 32 interviews, doctors mentioned that patients expected antibiotics and would go elsewhere if they didn't get them. Clinic targets were mentioned explicitly in 11 interviews. The observational data was consistent with this: antibiotics were prescribed in 58% of consultations for upper respiratory symptoms, and in 71% of consultations in which the patient asked for a specific medicine. Consultations in which antibiotics were prescribed were on average 1.4 minutes shorter.

Analysis of the policy documents revealed a gradual shift in how the target population of the insurance scheme was described. Documents from 2005 to 2010 refer to "the poor" and "below poverty line families". Documents from 2011 onwards increasingly refer to "vulnerable groups" and, after 2016, to "the missing middle", a phrase which first appears in a circular on the expansion of the scheme to informal workers. Informal workers was named explicitly in only 6 of the 47 documents. Monitoring indicators changed less than the stated objectives: enrolment numbers remained the main indicator throughout.

Purchases of alcohol fell by 7.6% (95% CI 4.9 to 10.3) in households in the intervention region relative to the comparison regions. The reduction was largest among households in the top decile of baseline purchasing (13.1%), and was concentrated on cheap cider, own-brand spirits and high-strength lager, the products most affected by the minimum price. Among households in the lowest income tercile, the reduction was 9.4% for the heaviest purchasers and close to zero for the lightest. Expenditure on alcohol did not change significantly in any income group, so heavy-purchasing households spent about the same and received less alcohol for it.

The second theme, being caught in between, captured the tension CHWs felt when supervisors' targets conflicted with what households needed. Several participants described having to choose between completing the required number of household visits and spending more time with a family in crisis. One participant explained: "If I stay one hour with the mother whose baby is sick, then I miss three houses, and in the meeting they only ask about the three houses." Participants felt that there work was judged by numbers rather than by what they actually did for families. Some participants described falsifying the visit register.

Adolescents at schools that started at 9:00 slept on average 34 minutes longer on school nights than those at schools starting at 8:15 (Table 3). The difference was driven by later wake times, bedtimes did not differ. Sleep on weekend nights was similar in both groups, which suggest that the difference on school nights is not due to differences in underlying sleep preference. Students at later-starting schools also reported less daytime sleepiness. These findings were robust to adjustment for age, sex, socioeconomic status and screen use.

Participants who left the scheme described a series of small problems rather than a single decision. The first problem was usually a delay in the reimbursement of a claim. The second problem, in many cases, was that the nearest empanelled hospital refused admission or asked for a deposit. The third problem was a family member's experience. These problems accumulated over time. This is evident from the fact that most participants could not identify the exact moment when they stopped using the card, and many said they still had it but "kept it in the cupboard".

Social network analysis showed significant changes. The density of the networks increased from 0.21 to 0.34 which shows that tenants became highly more connected. The number of isolates decreased dramatically. This proves that housing first is effective for social integration. In addition, it was found that the networks became more homogeneous with regard to housing status. Tenants who had been homeless for longer had smaller networks at all time points, and the tenants who were older also reported fewer new ties. Contact with family members increased slightly, from a median of one family member at baseline to two at eighteen months.

Experiences of the transition to remote teaching varied considerably between teachers. Younger teachers generally described the move as manageable and some described it as an opportunity to try new methods. Older teachers more often described it as exhausting. However, this pattern was not universal, and two of the oldest teachers in the sample were among the most enthusiastic about online teaching. Teachers in schools where most students lacked a device described their work during this period as "teaching into a void", since only a handful of students joined each session.

Across the eleven oral history interviews, the dispute is remembered primarily as a story about the town's women. Interviewees repeatedly described the women who ran the soup kitchen and who confronted the strike-breakers at the station, and several attributed the dispute's length to their determination. The documentary record supports part of this account: the strike committee's minutes record the soup kitchen's accounts and thank its organisers by name. It does not record any confrontation at the station, which appears in the interviews in four different versions, each set in a different month.

Our findings suggest that riders experience time on the platform as a resource they must constantly manage but cannot control. This is consistent with earlier accounts of piece-rate work, but it differs in one important respect: the rate of work is set not by a supervisor but by an algorithm whose rules riders could only guess at. This matters for policy. Proposals to guarantee a minimum hourly income for riders often count only the time spent delivering, yet riders in our study considered waiting time to be working time, and many arranged their entire day around it.

The results of this study clearly prove that mindfulness courses are highly effective for improving student wellbeing. Students who took the course reported less distress at the end of the course, and this definitely shows that universities should offer mindfulness to all students. Although the effect was smaller at six months and had disappeared by twelve months, this is probably due to the students stopping their practice.

It may possibly be the case that the association between trust and vaccination completion could perhaps be explained, at least in part, by the fact that caregivers who trust volunteers might be more likely to attend vaccination sessions. It is also possible that the relationship may run in the other direction. Caregivers who have completed vaccination might potentially develop more trust as a result of their contacts with volunteers.

This study found that SHG membership has a positive impact on the decision making power of rural women. This finding is in line with the findings of earlier studies conducted in other states. The increase in participation in decisions related to children's education may be because women now contribute to household income through the SHG activities, which gives them a say in the household. However, in the decisions regarding the purchase of land, the participation of women is still very low. This shows that the patriarchal structures in the rural society are still very much intact and the SHG alone cannot change the same.

A central finding of this chapter is that the dispute was sustained less by the formal organisations of the labour movement than by informal networks of sympathy that extended well beyond the textile districts, networks that are almost invisible in the union records on which most historians of the period have relied, but that appear clearly once the strike-fund ledger is read alongside the railway parcel books and the letters that accompanied each remittance. If this pattern held for other disputes of the period, then the conventional chronology, in which effective solidarity across trades begins only with the federations of the 1890s, may need to be pushed back by at least a decade.

The absence of an effect of benefit duration on the quality of the next job is notable. A common argument for longer benefits is that they allow workers to search for a better match rather than accepting the first offer. We find no evidence of this, at least as measured by wages and industry. One possible explanation is that in a labour market with a large informal sector, workers who are recieving benefits may also be working informally, so that the extra time is not spent searching at all. We cannot test this directly, because informal work is not observed in our data.

This is important because it suggests that the way consent is currently obtained may not protect participants in the way it is intended to. This has implications for ethics committees. This is particularly relevant for research in rural areas, where this kind of household decision making is common. Ethics committees could consider requiring researchers to describe how they will address this.

The finding that teachers express different beliefs about ability in different settings challenges the common practice of measuring mindset with a single questionnaire. If beliefs depend on the task at hand, then a teacher may hold a growth mindset when discussing an individual student's work and act on a fixed mindset when assigning students to sets. Interventions that aim to change teachers' beliefs may therefore need to target the institutional decisions, such as setting, where fixed-ability talk is most common, rather than teachers' general attitudes.

The reduction in alcohol purchases among the heaviest purchasing households is consistent with the intended aim of the policy, which was to target cheap, strong alcohol. Concerns that the policy would place an unfair burden on low-income moderate drinkers are not supported by our findings: low-income households who bought little alcohol before the policy changed their purchases very little and did not spend more. However, low-income heavy purchasers spent the same amount of money for less alcohol. Whether this represents a welfare gain, because of the health benefits of drinking less, or a welfare loss, because these households have less money for other goods, depends on assumptions about rationality that our data cannot resolve.

In this study, we found that loneliness is common among older adults even when they live with family, and I think this challenges the assumption that multigenerational households protect against isolation. Our qualitative data suggest that what matters is not the presence of others but whether the older person is included in decisions. I would argue that this is consistent with theories of loneliness which emphasise the quality rather than the quantity of relationships. We therefore recommend that interventions focus on family communication.

There are a number of possible explanations for the finding that talking about school at home was associated with reading progress while other forms of involvement was not. The first explanation is that talking about school might increase children's motivation. The second explanation is that it might improve children's oral language, which supports reading. The third explanation is that it reflects family characteristics which were not measured in this study and that the association is not causal. The data does not allow us to distinguish between these explanations.

The cost message produced a small additional reduction in missed appointments beyond that produced by a standard reminder. This finding is broadly consistent with trials of social-norm and loss-framed messages in other public services, which have typically found small effects. Because the cost message added nothing to the cost of sending a reminder, even a small affect is worth having. Services considering reminders should note, though, that most of the benefit came from sending a reminder at all.

The implementation of the strategy of the utilisation of community health workers for the delivery of mental health interventions has been the subject of the consideration of many policy makers. The findings of this study have implications for the development of the training of such workers. The provision of supervision and the establishment of referral pathways should be given consideration in the planning of such programmes.

Our findings regarding social networks is more complicated than either the optimistic or the pessimistic accounts in the literature would suggest. Tenants lost many ties to people still on the street, but this was not experienced simply as a loss, nor simply as a gain. Several tenants described deliberately reducing contact to protect their tenancy, while missing the people they had distanced themselves from. Housing programmes might therefore consider how to support tenants in maintaining relationships safely, for example by providing spaces where tenants can meet friends outside their flat.

Our interview findings show that the first-year design project is a key site where women experience marginalisation. Because all women in our sample described this experience, it is clear that gendered task allocation is the main cause of women leaving engineering. Departments should therefore restructure group projects. This would solve the problem of women leaving engineering, and it would also improve the experience of male students, who would learn a wider range of skills. Universities that fail to do this are actively discriminating against women.

The rise in catastrophic expenditure among the poorest rural households is concerning, especially since it occurred during a period when the national insurance scheme was being expanded. One explanation is that the scheme covers hospital admissions, whereas most out-of-pocket spending in poor rural households is on outpatient medicines, which the scheme does not cover. Another explanation is that poor rural households are less likely to be enrolled. Both explanations point toward the same policy conclusion, but they has different implications for implementation.

Although the effect of later school start times on sleep duration was consistent with studies conducted elsewhere, it is worth noting that the absolute size of the effect was modest. Thirty-four minutes is a meaningful amount of additional sleep, but adolescents in both groups still slept less then the recommended eight to ten hours. Later start times should therefore be seen as one part of a broader approach, rather than a solution in themselves.

The doctors in this study were acutely aware of the problem of antimicrobial resistance, and many of them spoke about it with evident concern; yet the same doctors prescribed antibiotics in well over half of consultations for respiratory symptoms, and their explanations for doing so placed the decision within a set of commercial and relational pressures that no single clinician could resist alone. This gap between knowledge and practice is not, therefore, a gap in education, and interventions that focus on informing doctors about resistance are unlikely to change prescribing on their own.

The study has shown that the main reason for discontinuation of the digital payments is the delay in settlement. This is a technical problem which could be easily solved by the banks. The study has also shown that the transaction charges is a burden for the small retailers. The government should take steps to reduce the charges for the small retailers. The fear of tax scrutiny is also an important reason. It is the need of the hour that the government should create awareness among the retailers about the benefits of digital payments.

These findings must be interpreted in light of the historical context in which the policy documents were written. The shift in language from "the poor" to "vulnerable groups" coincided with the government's adoption of a broader social protection agenda, and it may reflect a genuine broadening of the scheme's ambitions. It may equally reflect a desire to avoid the administrative burden of identifying poor households, which had proved contentious. The documents alone cannot tell us which of these motivations dominated, and interviews with officials involved in drafting them would be needed to answer this.

The moral distress described by CHWs in this study shares some features with moral distress among nurses, notably the sense of being prevented from acting on one's values by institutional constraints. However, there are also differences. Unlike hospital nurses, CHWs work alone in households, often in their own neighbourhood, so the people whose needs they cannot meet are also their neighbours. Several participants described meeting the families they had not been able to help at the market or at religious gatherings. This proximity may make moral distress more persistent, as there is no clear separation between work and home.

In conclusion, the findings indicates that there is a need for more research. Future research should be conducted with larger samples and in different settings. It would also be useful to use longitudinal designs. In addition, future studies should include the perspectives of other stakeholders such as teachers, parents and policy makers. Qualitative research would also be useful to understand the reasons behind the findings.

Our estimate of the effect of benefit duration is smaller than most estimates from Western Europe, where an additional month of benefits is typically found to lengthen unemployment by one to two weeks. Seen in that light, our estimate of six weeks for six additional months is at the lower end. This is what one would expect in a labour market where many workers can supplement or replace benefits with informal earnings, so that the incentive effect of benefits on formal job search is weaker. It also implies that extending benefit duration in this setting is cheaper, in terms of lost employment, than the European evidence would suggest.

The participants in this study clearly felt that thematic analysis papers are poorly reported, and we found that 72% of the papers we reviewed did not describe who did the coding. This confirms that the method is fundamentally flawed. Researchers should stop using thematic analysis unless they can justify it. Journals should also refuse to publish thematic analyses which do not report who did the coding, how many coders was involved and how disagreements were resolved, since without this information readers cannot judge the trustworthiness of the findings.

It is interesting to note that the remote teaching experiences of older teachers did not conform to the expected pattern. Two of the oldest teachers were among those who are most enthusiastic. One possible reason for this is that these teachers had previously worked in distance education programmes in the 1990s. Another possible reason is that they has fewer caring responsibilities at home. This suggests that age itself may be less important than prior experience and personal circumstances, a finding which challenges the common narrative of the digitally resistant older teacher.

Taken together, our results imply that minimum wage increases may reduce hours even when they do not reduce employment, which would mean that headcount-based studies understate the costs of the policy for workers. However, a single employer is not a market, and the firm we studied may have responded differently from smaller retailers with less flexible rosters. We also could not observe whether workers whose hours fell took up second jobs, which would offset some of the loss in earnings.

Our findings provide strong evidence that loneliness among older adults is primarily caused by exclusion from family decision-making. As explained above, the interviews showed that excluded participants felt lonely. This is a very significant finding which has never been reported before in the literature. It fundamentally changes how we should think about loneliness in this population. Previous studies have focused on living arrangements, on widowhood, and on health status, but none of them have considered the role of decision-making within the family, which our study has shown to be the key factor. In the light of these findings it is recommended that all health workers who visit older adults at home should ask about whether the older person is included in family decisions, and that family counselling should be provided where they are not, because otherwise the older person will inevitably become lonely and this will lead to depression and to poorer physical health. Policy makers must recognise that the family is not automatically a source of support for older people and that loneliness can occur in the middle of a crowded household, which is something that has been overlooked for far too long in both research and policy.

The results of our study is in agreement with previous studies which have reported that adolescent sleep is affected by school start times. In our study the students slept 34 minutes more which is similar to what was found in previous studies. However, our study was done in a different country and so it adds to the evidence. One strength of our study is the large sample size. The study had some weaknesses as well which are discussed below.

Why did the remittances from distant towns arrive through chapels and public houses rather than through the unions? One answer is simply that the unions of the period were organised by trade, and miners or dockers had no formal reason to support textile workers. But the letters suggest a further answer. Many of them describe the senders as former mill workers, or as the children of mill workers, who had moved away in search of better wages and who maintained a sense of obligation to the towns they had left. Migration, in other words, created the network that solidarity later travelled along.

The disparity in prescribing between consultations in which patients asked for a specific medicine and those in which they did not is consistent with the doctors' accounts, but it should be interpreted carefully. Patients who asked for a medicine may have had more severe symptoms, and I did not record any clinical measures that would allow this to be checked. Nonetheless, the combination of observational and interview data in this study gives a more convincing picture than either source alone, since the doctors' explanations were offered independently of the prescribing data and the two point in the same direction.

Compared to the findings of previous studies, the rates of participation in decisions found in the present study is higher. This might be because of the longer duration of SHG membership of the respondents in the present study, as most of them have been members for more than five years. It might also be because of the active role of the NGO in the study area which conducts regular trainings on gender issues. Thus it can be concluded that the duration of membership and the support of NGOs are the important factors for empowerment of women.

Seen from the perspective of the women who left, the problem was not engineering but the version of engineering they met in the first year. Several described returning to technical work later, in programming or in design roles, where they found the collaborative culture they had expected from the start. These accounts complicate the language of a 'leaky pipeline', which implies that women who leave a degree are lost to the field. Some of them were redirected rather than lost, although the path they took to technical work was longer and, in several cases, more expensive.

This study have some important implications for practice. Firstly, ethics committees should require researchers to explain how they will obtain consent in settings where decisions is made collectively. Secondly, consent forms should be shorter and should be explained verbally. Thirdly, researchers should be trained in culturally appropriate ways to approach households. Fourthly, there should be a mechanism for participants to withdraw consent after the researcher has left.

The finding that tenants who lost their tenancies had both invited friends to stay deserves careful interpretation. It would be easy to read this as evidence that ties to homeless friends threaten tenancies, and therefore that programmes should discourage them. But two cases cannot support such a conclusion, and tenants who maintained ties without losing their tenancy were far more numerous. The more defensible conclusion is that tenancy rules about guests can turn an act of loyalty into a breach of contract, and that programmes should examine those rules.

Overall, the reminder trial and the qualitative interviews with clinic staff points in the same direction: missed appointments are mostly forgotten appointments, not refusals. That is good news for services, as forgetting is easier to fix than reluctance. It also suggests that the moralising tone sometimes found in public campaigns about missed appointments, which treat non-attenders as careless or ungrateful, is misplaced.

Background: School-based counselling is widely offered to adolescents, but little is known about what happens in counselling sessions. Methods: We audio-recorded 96 sessions conducted by 14 counsellors in 11 secondary schools and coded the content of each session using a framework developed for this study. Results: Academic pressure was the most common presenting concern (41% of sessions), followed by family conflict (27%) and peer relationships (19%). Counsellors spent a median of 38% of session time giving advice, and only 9% of sessions included any structured technique. Conclusions: School counselling in these settings is predominantly advice-giving. Training in brief structured interventions could make better use of the limited time available.

This study examines the effect of a regional minimum wage increase on the hours worked by part-time retail employees. Using payroll records from a large retail employer with stores on both sides of a regional border, we compares changes in weekly hours for part-time workers in stores affected by the increase with workers in unaffected stores. We find that the increase reduced weekly hours by 1.3 hours (around 6%) on average, with no change in the probability of employment. The reduction was larger for workers with less than one year of tenure. These results suggests that employment-based estimates may understate the effect of minimum wages on workers' earnings.

Moral distress has been extensively studied among nurses but rarely among community health workers (CHWs). This qualitative study explored experiences of moral distress among CHWs in a peri-urban district. I interviewed 22 CHWs and analysed the data using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes were developed: knowing the household, being caught in between, and carrying it home. CHWs described distress arising from conflicts between supervisors' targets and households' needs, made more acute by the fact that they lived among the families they served. Some CHWs coped by falsifying visit records. Findings suggest that performance management systems for CHWs should be redesigned to recognise time spent with families in crisis.

The aim of this paper was to examine the reasons for the discontinuation of the use of digital payments by small retailers following an initial adoption. A total of 52 retailers in three cities who had adopted and then discontinued digital payments was interviewed. The results revealed that delay in settlement, transaction charges and fear of tax scrutiny were the main reasons. The findings of the study clearly establishes that the digital payment ecosystem is not suitable for small retailers. The study recommends that banks and government should take necessary steps for the same.

Informal networks of support are central to how industrial disputes were sustained, yet historians have reconstructed them mainly through union records. This article follow a single regional textile dispute of the 1880s through a strike-fund ledger, railway parcel books, and letters that accompanied remittances to the strike committee. It shows that, after the first two months, support came increasingly from distant towns with no textile industry, collected in chapels and public houses by people who described themselves as former mill workers or their children. I argue that labour migration created the networks along which solidarity later travelled, and that the chronology of cross-trade solidarity in the period should be revised accordingly.

Background: Missed appointments waste clinical capacity in public dental services. We tested whether text message reminders, and reminders mentioning the cost of a missed appointment, reduce non-attendance. Methods: Individually randomised three-arm trial in 14 clinics (n = 3,612). Results: Missed appointments were 15.3% with no reminder, 12.1% with a standard reminder and 10.4% with a cost reminder. Conclusion: Reminders reduce missed appointments, and mentioning cost adds a small further benefit at no extra cost.

Loneliness in old age is generally considered to be a problem of people who live alone. In this mixed methods study, we examined loneliness among 62 older adults who were living in multigenerational households in two towns. Loneliness was measured with the UCLA scale and in-depth interviews were conducted with a subsample of 20 participants. Loneliness were common, and it was higher among widowed participants, women, and those without their own room. The number of family members in the household is not associated with loneliness. Interviews showed that exclusion from family decision-making was a central feature of participants' experience of loneliness. This study proves that living with family does not protect against loneliness and that family communication interventions are urgently needed.

Research on teachers' beliefs about intelligence has relied heavily on questionnaires. We recorded 41 hours of mathematics department planning meetings and interviewed 18 teachers about named students in four secondary schools, and coded 1,184 statements about student ability. Teachers linked ability to effort or teaching in 61% of interview statements but in only 34% of planning-meeting statements, where fixed-ability talk clustered around decisions about setting. Teachers' expressed beliefs depend on the institutional task at hand, and interventions to change them may need to target the decisions where fixed-ability reasoning is used.

In the present study, an attempt has been made to study the impact of Self Help Groups on the empowerment of rural women. The study was conducted in two blocks of the district with a sample of 240 SHG members selected by multi-stage random sampling. Data were collected through a pre-tested interview schedule and analysed using percentages, chi-square test and Garrett ranking. The study found that after joining the SHG there was a significant increase in the participation of women in household decision making, mobility and participation in gram sabha meetings. However, participation in decisions regarding purchase and sale of land remained low. Lack of time, family restrictions and illiteracy was ranked as the major constraints. The study concludes that SHGs are playing a very important role in the empowerment of women but more efforts is required.

This thesis investigates how public health insurance schemes in three countries defined the populations they intended to cover, and how those definitions changed as the schemes expanded. Drawing on 47 policy documents, I trace the shift from targeting "the poor" to targeting "vulnerable groups" and finally "the missing middle." I argue that each change in language accompanied a change in how eligibility was administered and who was responsible for it. The thesis contributes to debates about universal health coverage by showing that the expansion of coverage is as much a process of reclassification as of financing.

This study has several limitations.
