First, the sample was recruited through community centres and pensioner's associations, so the most isolated older adults, who may be the loneliest, are likely to be under-represented. Second, the UCLA loneliness scale was developed in a different cultural context and has not been validated in Marathi; some items, particularly those referring to "companionship", may have been understood differently. Third, the cross-sectional design mean that we cannot establish whether exclusion from decisions leads to loneliness or whether lonely older adults withdraw from family life.

There are some limitations of this study which needs to be acknowledged. The sample size was small and the participants were recruited from only one university, so the findings may not be generalisable. Also the data was self-reported which can lead to bias. Another limitation is that the study was cross-sectional and therefore causal relationships cannot be established. Despite these limitation, the study provides useful insights.

My presence in the consultation room is the most important limitation of the observational data. Doctors knew I was studying prescribing, and it is likely that they prescribed fewer antibiotics while I was watching than they would otherwise have done. If so, the true prescribing rate is higher than the 58% I observed, which would strengthen rather than weaken the argument of this chapter. A second limitation is that clinics agreed to take part, and owners who were more concerned about their reputation may have declined.

A limitation of our approach is that the register only records formal employment. Workers who move into informal work are therefore indistinguishable from workers who remain unemployed or who leave the labour force. If eligible workers are more likely to take informal jobs while receiving benefits, which seems plausible, then our estimate overstates the effect of benefits on total time without work, though it remains a valid estimate of the effect on time without formal work, which is what matters for social security contributions.

Like all archival studies this research is limited by what has survived. The strike-fund ledger is complete but the letters are not, and it is impossible to know how many were lost or what they said. The railway parcel books survive for only two of the five stations in the district. Its therefore likely that the network of support was even wider than I have been able to show. The oral history interviews, as discussed in chapter 2, tells us more about memory than about the dispute itself.

This thesis set out to understand how riders on food delivery platforms experience and manage their working time. It has shown that riders treats waiting as work, organise their days around order targets rather than hours, and develop shared, partial theories of how the platform allocates orders. These findings matter for current debates about minimum earnings guarantees, which typically count only time spent on active deliveries. A guarantee that excludes waiting time would leave out much of what riders themselves count as their working day.

In conclusion, the present study has made an attempt to understand the various problems faced by the retailers in the usage of digital payments. It is concluded that delay in settlement is the major problem. It is hoped that the findings of the study will be useful to the policy makers, banks and the retailers. More studies are required in this area in other states also so that a comprehensive picture can be obtained regarding the same.

Overall, this study demonstrates that minimum unit pricing achieved what it was designed to do. It reduced alcohol purchases most among the households who bought the most, and it did so without increasing the spending of low-income households who drink moderately. The policy did not, however, reduce spending among low-income heavy purchasers, and the welfare consequences for this group remain uncertain. Future evaluations should link purchase data to health outcomes, so that the benefits of reduced drinking can be weighed against the financial pressure the policy may place on these households.

To conclude, the findings of this study clearly show that trust is the most important factor in vaccination and that it is absolutely essential that all immunisation programmes in the country must focus on building trust. If programmes invest in trust, vaccine hesitancy will be eliminated. Volunteers should be given more training and more incentives so that they can build the trust of the caregivers.

This research suggests that the experience of first-year group projects plays a substantial role in women's decisions to leave engineering, though it is unlikely to be the only factor. Changes to how projects are structured, such as rotating technical roles and assessing individual contributions, is low-cost and could be piloted within a single academic year. Further research should follow women who leave to establish where they go, since the evidence from our interviews suggests that many remain in technical work by other routes.

Chapter 3: Community health workers and the ethics of everyday care. The previous chapter showed that the literature on moral distress has developed almost entirely in hospital settings. Some studies has looked at primary care. But no study, to my knowledge, has examined moral distress among community health workers in their own neighbourhoods, and this is a gap. This chapter attempt to fill it, by drawing on interviews with 22 CHWs and on six months of fieldwork in their district. I begin by describing the setting and the work CHWs do, before turning to the three themes which structure the rest of the chapter.

Existing accounts of nineteenth-century industrial disputes say a great deal about strike committees, unions and employers, and remarkably little about the ordinary people, often hundreds of miles away, whose small contributions kept strikers fed. That silence is partly a matter of sources: union records survive in organised archives, whereas the letters and ledger entries that document informal support are scattered and incomplete. It is also a matter of method, since a single town's records cannot reveal a network that spanned many towns. This chapter addresses both problems, assembling records from five county archives to reconstruct, week by week, where the money supporting one dispute came from.

Chapter 4 – Literature Review. There has been a lot of research on the topic of undermatching. In this chapter I will review this research. Some research has looked at information interventions. Some research has looked at financial aid. Some research has looked at the role of schools. There is less research on completion. Hence this study is very much needed and will make a important contribution to the field.

Recommendations. (1) The ministry should extend the free medicines list to cover the twenty outpatient medicines that account for most out-of-pocket spending in poor rural households, and fund district stores accordingly. (2) Facility managers should be required to report stock-outs weekly, and patients sent to private pharmacies during a stock-out should be reimbursed at the public price. (3) Insurance enrolment drives should prioritise rural households in the poorest quintile, where coverage remains lowest. (4) Progress should be monitored using the share of households facing catastrophic spending, not only the number enrolled.

Policy Recommendations: It is recommended that the concerned authorities may kindly take the necessary steps for the reduction of the transaction charges levied on small retailers. It is also recommended that the settlement period should be reduced to same day. Awareness programmes should be conducted by banks for the retailers regarding the benefits of digital payments. It is very important and urgent that the tax department should clarify that the digital payments will not lead to any harassment of small traders. All these steps will definitely increase the adoption of the digital payments.

Response to Reviewer 2, comment 3: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. The reviewer is correct that the original manuscript did not explain how the second coder was trained. We have now added a paragraph to the Methods (page 9, lines 14–22) explaining that the second coder was trained using five transcripts that were not part of the study data, and that agreement was discussed after each one. We have not calculated a kappa statistic, as we consider inter-coder agreement statistics to be inconsistant with the reflexive approach to thematic analysis that we adopted; we explain this reasoning in the revised text.

Reviewer 1 comment: The authors should discuss whether the results could be explained by selection into later-starting schools. Response: Thank you for this important point. We agree that this is a potential concern. We have added a sentence about this. As explained in the manuscript, students were assigned to schools by catchment area so we think selection is unlikely. We have also did a sensitivity analysis which adjusted for neighbourhood deprivation and the results were similar. We hope this addresses the reviewers concern.

Comment 4: The reviewer asked us to clarify why the sample was restricted to workers aged 35 to 45. Response: The restriction follows from the regression discontinuity design. Workers far from the age-40 threshold differ from each other in many ways besides benefit eligibility, and including them would make the estimate depend heavily on the functional form chosen. We now say this explicitly in Section 3.2 and report, in Appendix Table A4, estimates using windows of 38–42 and 33–47 years. The point estimates are 37 and 44 days respectively, both close to the main estimate.

The overall aim of this project is to determine whether later school start times improve adolescents' sleep, mood and attendance in a setting outside North America. Aim 1 is to estimate the effect of start time on school-night sleep duration using actigraphy in 1,200 students across 24 schools. Aim 2 is to examine whether any change in sleep is accompanied by changes in self-reported mood and in recorded attendance. Aim 3 is to understand, through interviews with students, parents and school leaders, what makes a change in start time feasible or difficult to sustain. Together, these aims will give school authorities the evidence they need to decide whether a change is worth the disruption.

Specific Aims. Antibiotic over-prescribing in private primary care is a major driver of AMR in the region. The proposed project will develop and test a intervention to reduce over-prescribing which will address the commercial pressures identified in our previous research. Aim 1: To co-design, with clinic owners and doctors, a package which includes a patient-facing information leaflet, a prescription audit and feedback and a revised consultation fee structure. Aim 2: To pilot the package in 10 clinics and assess its feasibility. Aim 3: To estimate the effect on prescribing, which we expect will be reduced by atleast 30% compared to control clinics, in a cluster randomised trial.
